title: Nobunaga, Hideyoshi, Ieyasu and the Cuckoo: Why None Wrote the Haiku
description:
On the night of Bunsei 4, 11th month, 17th day (December 11, 1821, Gregorian), a kasshi day in the sixty-day cycle, Matsura Seizan, the retired lord of Hirado, began writing Kasshi Yawa. One entry tells of a hototogisu, a small cuckoo, that someone sent and that would not sing. Today Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu are each said to have told it a verse. Did they really write them?

In volume 53, leaf 7, before the three verses, Kasshi Yawa records what someone said during a night talk: probably made up and attributed to them, but true to each man's nature. The earliest version found so far is in Mimibukuro by Negishi Yasumori, who died in 1815: there Ieyasu says "listen when it sings," and the renga master Jōha adds "not singing is fine too." Negishi also writes that he does not know whether it is an old tale or someone's invention.

Nearly every book from Meiji on calls the verses a later invention, yet their wording kept changing: in 1909 Ieyasu's verse already read "let's wait until it sings," by 1910 all three were close to today's wording, and a 1935 ethics teaching guide quoting Kasshi Yawa changed the character for "wait" in Ieyasu's verse. We did not find which book fixed today's version, and who wrote the verses is still unknown.

Kasshi Yawa is quoted from the Matsura family's 1900 printing in the Database of Pre-modern Japanese Works (text only), Mimibukuro from the six-volume Nihon Geirin Sōsho edition, and later books from the National Diet Library Digital Collections. We did not open the Tōyō Bunko or ten-volume editions, whose wording may differ; the origin of "Ieyasu's testament" rests on secondary sources; "found so far" means within what we searched. Narration dates follow the old calendar; "we think" marks this channel's view; references are below.

The illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters not meant to resemble anyone, modern researchers are not drawn, and the bird stays unharmed throughout.

Information as of 2026-10-20

hh102.text: Matsura Seizan, retired lord of Hirado, had a guest.

hh103.text: Shogunate rector Hayashi Jussai watched him forge; they talked late.

hh104.text: That night, the old lord began a notebook.

hh105.text: It was a kasshi day, so he called it Kasshi Yawa.

hh106.text: One entry: someone sent a hototogisu, a small cuckoo.

hh107.text: But it wouldn't sing a single note.

hh108.text: Today it's said the three unifiers each told it a line.

hh109.text: Before the three verses, Seizan noted someone's remark.

hh110.text: Another shogunate official also noted the three and the bird.

hh112.text: In Shōwa 10, a school ethics class made it a lesson.

hh113.text: Did Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu really write these verses?

hh201.text: Volume 53, leaf 7: before the verses, someone already answered:

hh202.text: Probably pinned on them by others; still, true to each man.

hh203.text: Pinned on them: made up in their name.

hh204.text: Was it Seizan who said this?

hh205.text: No. The book only says "a certain person": someone.

hh206.text: We read the 100-volume main series the Matsura family printed itself in Meiji 33.

hh207.text: After that remark come the bird and the verses.

hh209.text: To whom, or when, the book never says.

hh210.text: The verses aren't signed Nobunaga, Hideyoshi or Ieyasu.

hh212.text: Their titles. Oda Ufu: If it won't sing, kill it.

hh213.text: Hō Taikō: Won't sing? I'll make it sing.

hh214.text: Dai Gongen-sama: If it won't sing, wait until it does.

hh215.text: Ufu means Minister of the Right; Dai Gongen is the god's title Ieyasu got after death.

hh216.text: Even the bird's name varies: another oft-cited copy spells it three ways;

hh217.text: the Meiji edition we read spells it the same in all three.

hh218.text: Its proofreader: the copy had doubtful words; they checked sources, asked friends, then fixed them.

hh219.text: But that's not all: two more verses follow.

hh220.text: One: If it won't sing, send it to the bird shop. The other: If it won't sing, just keep it.

hh221.text: The book says: out of discretion, and since they're made up, no authors named.

hh223.text: The book says not a word.

hh224.text: The entries on either side are odd tidbits unrelated to the three.

hh225.text: So was Seizan the first to write down these three and this bird?

hh301.text: No. The earliest found so far is that other official: Negishi Yasumori.

hh302.text: He died in Bunka 12, before Seizan began his night talks.

hh303.text: From his time as Sado magistrate, he kept notes for some 30 years: Mimibukuro.

hh304.text: This entry's title: at a renga gathering, a man's true heart shows itself.

hh307.text: An old tale, or someone's invention? I don't know.

hh308.text: Remember the bird someone sent? Here, nobody sends a bird.

hh309.text: The three are together: it's the 4th month, and no cuckoo yet.

hh310.text: The old 4th month is about today's May, just when cuckoos should arrive.

hh311.text: Nobunaga's verse means the same as Seizan's.

hh312.text: Hideyoshi: Won't sing? I'll make it, and listen.

hh313.text: Negishi even left a space before Ieyasu, in respect.

hh315.text: If it won't sing, listen when it does.

hh316.text: This one has no "wait"; that "wait" is only in Seizan's entry.

hh317.text: Jōha, the top renga poet of the day, was there and added a fourth:

hh319.text: Negishi says each verse shows its man: Ieyasu gentle, Hideyoshi generous, Nobunaga impatient.

hh320.text: Not even the biggest cast yet.

hh321.text: Sometime in Meiji 10-19, a hand copy from old essays even adds Maeda Toshiie;

hh322.text: and sets it at Nobunaga's banquet in Azuchi Castle.

hh323.text: Some joked about it. A Taishō-era senryu scholar dated one senryu to the Bunka era:

hh324.text: one cuckoo yields three verses: wisdom, benevolence, courage.

hh325.text: If that date is right, the verses reached commoners' senryu before Seizan began writing.

hh326.text: Whether it or Mimibukuro came first is unclear.

hh327.text: In Meiji, did books still say it may be made up?

hh401.text: They did. A Meiji 34 self-improvement book wrote: probably a tale someone made up.

hh402.text: But it went on: read the three verses and you can picture the three men.

hh403.text: It also wrote the bird's "sing" as "weep";

hh404.text: and signed them with their real names.

hh405.text: In Meiji 37, a teaching dictionary for school textbooks labeled them "On Nobunaga," "On Hideyoshi," "On Ieyasu": assessments.

hh407.text: Life is like walking a long road with a heavy load; never hurry.

hh409.text: A Meiji 42 youth guide also said: a later invention.

hh410.text: Yet the wording kept changing: now the three meet and wait long, but the bird stays silent.

hh411.text: Ieyasu's already read "let's wait until it sings," as today.

hh413.text: In Meiji 43, a speaking-and-writing guide for school readers wrote the three verses

hh414.text: almost exactly as we say them today.

hh415.text: It, too, only said: tradition credits them to the three.

hh416.text: In Taishō 15, the scholar who dated that senryu to Bunka also noted a view:

hh417.text: likely a later sketch of the three, using the cuckoo.

hh418.text: In his version, the scene changed again: a set-theme poetry meet.

hh419.text: Strangest to us: openly called made up, yet still used to teach the men's character.

hh420.text: So which book fixed today's version?

hh501.text: We found no such book; even in Shōwa 10, the verses were still being altered.

hh502.text: Remember that ethics lesson? It was called "The Waiting Heart."

hh503.text: Its first section: someone speaks of the hearts of Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu.

hh505.text: Its teacher's guide cited Kasshi Yawa for them,

hh506.text: and quoted the two extra verses and the "no authors" line, too.

hh508.text: No. Ieyasu's "wait" was swapped for the character in the lesson's name.

hh509.text: Remember the Meiji proofreader? This change wasn't to correct, but to match the lesson.

hh510.text: Five years on, a history reader was blunter: would three warring heroes really cozy up to verse on one bird?

hh511.text: He said it must be a later fabrication.

hh512.text: And the "heavy load on a long road" printed with the verses in Meiji 37?

hh513.text: Researchers think it was pinned on Ieyasu only in late Edo.

hh514.text: So, the opening question: did they write these verses?

hh515.text: Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu died in 1582, 1598 and 1616;

hh516.text: the two Edo notebooks found so far come some 200 years later.

hh517.text: No record from their own time mentions these cuckoo verses.

hh518.text: Who really wrote them is still unknown.

hh519.text: Remember "true to each man" from that night talk?

hh520.text: We think the verses lasted 200 years on that alone: they sound like them.

hh521.text: None of the three wrote them. This file is closed.

hh522.text: What would you say to this bird that won't sing?

hh523.text: We only cover what the records hold. Subscribe and open the files with us.
